U.S. Midterm Elections · 3 November 2026

The Midterm Effect

What 21 midterm cycles reveal about the S&P 500, and whether 2026 can extend the streak

Prepared by

Alia Akram

Senior Account Manager · Mubasher Capital Derivatives

01 · The Event

Election Day: Tuesday, 3 November 2026

What is on the ballot

All 435 House seats and roughly one-third of the Senate, deciding control of Congress for the rest of the presidential term.

Why markets care

Control of Congress shapes taxes, government spending and regulation, the policy inputs behind earnings expectations.

The question for investors

History points to a strong post-election rally. Is 2026 set to follow the pattern, or break it?

A perfect post-midterm record since 1942

21/21

Through wars, recessions, oil shocks and rate-hiking cycles, every midterm since 1942 ended the following June with the index higher.

04 · The Record

Different datasets, the same conclusion

16.6%

Average S&P 500 gain in the year after a midterm election, since 1950

18.2%

Average 12-month gain after the 17 midterms since 1954, positive every time

16.9%

Average 12-month total return across the nine midterm cycles since 1990, all positive

15.5%

Average return from Election Day to 30 June, going back to 1950

Across start dates, time windows and methodologies, the period after a midterm has consistently ranked among the strongest stretches of the four-year presidential cycle.

08 · The 2026 Setup

What could support or derail the rally

History points to a post-election rally, but 2026 enters the vote with a longer list of risks than a typical midterm year. On the left, the forces that could reinforce the seasonal tailwind; on the right, the risks that could interrupt it.

Supportive

Corporate investment. Business spending has stayed resilient, paced by heavy AI capital expenditure.

Seasonality. The midterm fourth quarter and the two quarters after it have historically been the cycle’s strongest.

Policy clarity. The result removes a major source of uncertainty around taxes, spending and regulation.

On the watch list

AI and semiconductors. Valuations and the returns on AI capital spending are under scrutiny.

Inflation and energy. Persistent inflation and higher energy prices weigh on the outlook.

Rates and the Fed. Higher rates test confidence in the Fed’s ability to tame inflation.

Geopolitics. Geopolitical tensions remain elevated.

Sources: Fidelity Investments (October 2026); historical S&P 500 quarterly data since 1946.

10 · Reading the Result

What the balance of power could mean

Divided by design

Even a Democratic sweep leaves a Republican White House holding the veto, so the most likely practical outcome is divided government.

+23% versus +12%

Average S&P 500 gain in the post-midterm year under a Republican president with a split Congress, versus the average across all midterm outcomes (Morgan Stanley).

Either way

Divided government tends to limit sweeping legislative change, and post-midterm gains have historically come regardless of which party controls Congress.

10

11 · Policy Outlook

A Democratic sweep: the fiscal picture

The veto check

A sweep gives Democrats Congress, not the White House. The presidential veto would effectively block major Democratic legislation, so policy gridlock becomes the practical base case.

The deficit debate

Piper Sandler estimates Democratic proposals, including tariff repeal and restored Medicaid and ACA funding, would add about $5 trillion to deficits over a decade. Bond markets are signalling that fiscal excess will be met with higher borrowing costs.

Deadlines become events

Appropriations fights and the 2027 debt-limit negotiations would become market-relevant, alongside tougher oversight, confirmations and regulation. TD sees a slightly better chance of a debt-ceiling deal than under a split Congress.

11

12 · Policy Outlook

A Democratic sweep: the monetary picture

Tariffs and inflation

A Democratic Congress would likely push back harder on tariff escalation. Less tariff pressure could ease inflation over time, although tariff authority rests largely with the President.

The Fed path

Short-dated Treasuries already price a renewed tightening cycle of about a further 1% in rate hikes, driven by energy prices, tariffs and deficit spending rather than by the election itself.

Fed independence

Fed nominees need Senate confirmation, so a Democratic Senate would make appointments more contested. Amundi flags the risk of a constrained White House leaning on executive tools, including pressure on the Fed.

Market read-through: with a Democratic House close to fully priced, analysts expect a limited immediate reaction; a Republican sweep would be the bigger surprise.

12

13 · Policy Outlook

The gridlock scenario: a split Congress

Fiscal: deadlock

A Democratic House facing a Republican Senate makes fiscal deadlock the base case: little new legislation, but more uncertainty around spending deadlines, debt issuance, the term premium and the 2027 debt limit.

Monetary: status quo

A Republican Senate keeps confirmation of the President’s Fed nominees on a smoother path. Tariff authority stays with the White House, so trade-driven inflation risk does not disappear under divided government.

Markets: a familiar mix

Historically a supportive combination: under a Republican president with a split Congress, the S&P 500 has gained about 23% in the post-midterm year, versus 12% across all midterm outcomes.

Where it stands: priced at 26% on Kalshi, gridlock is the second most likely outcome. Because investors already expect some form of divided government, the immediate market reaction could be muted.

13

14 · The Big Question

Will 2026 be an anomaly?

The case for continuation

Every post-midterm window since 1942 has been positive, through wars, recessions and tightening cycles.

The vote removes a key source of policy uncertainty for taxes, spending and regulation.

Past cycles carried comparable risks, from 2018’s trade war to 2022’s 8%+ inflation, and still rallied.

What could break the streak

Elevated valuations leave less room for disappointment, especially in AI-linked leaders.

Persistent inflation could push the Fed toward a tighter path.

2026 enters the vote with double-digit gains, so there is less of a midterm drawdown to rebound from.

History sets the base rate; the 2026 backdrop sets the range of outcomes. A 21-for-21 record is a strong tailwind, not a guarantee.

16 · Positioning

Positioning around the vote

Directional exposure

Express a view on the post-election trend in U.S. equities through index derivatives, with greater capital efficiency than holding the underlying.

Event-risk hedging

Protect existing equity portfolios against election-week volatility while staying invested for a potential post-vote rally.

Higher-beta tilt

Higher-beta stocks have historically amplified post-midterm moves, adding upside potential alongside larger drawdown risk.

Risk discipline

Set entry levels, stop-losses and position sizes in advance. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses.
